title: A press or news page for a small company
metaTitle: A press page for a small company
excerpt: If you have little news, skip the newsroom. Link the few real mentions from the about page. An empty press room makes a small company look stalled.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass. The shop sign fits a piece about a small company that should stay open and honest about what it has to show.
caption: Open the door you actually have. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does a startup need a press page?
faqs.answer: Not until there is something real to put on it. A handful of genuine mentions belong on the about page, next to who you are. An empty newsroom, or a page of recycled product updates, looks like a company waiting for a story. Build the page when a journalist could land on it and find facts.

faqs.question: What should a small press page include?
faqs.answer: A short description of the company, a contact a human reads, and links to the actual mentions or announcements. Add a logo file and a one-line boilerplate only if people ask for them. Skip the embargo theater, the executive photo shoot you do not need, and the RSS feed of silence.

faqs.question: Where should news live if there is not enough for a section?
faqs.answer: On the about page, or in a single update on the journal when something real happened. Link out to the original article rather than copying it. Google's helpful-content guidance favors people-first pages with a clear purpose. A thin press section created to look established does not have that purpose.

markdown:
If you have little news, do not build a newsroom. A press page for startups is often a page that should not exist yet. Link the few real mentions from the about page. An empty press room looks like a stalled company. The nav item promises a public life. The page admits there isn't one.

You can be a serious company with no press. Many good ones are. The mistake is the costume: a "Media" section with a hero, a filter for years, and a grid of cards that say you will be right back. Visitors do not read that as humility. They read it as a launch that did not happen.

## When the page is a liability

Build a press page when a stranger could use it. A journalist, a partner, or a buyer who wants the boilerplate and the two places you have actually been mentioned. If those materials do not exist, the page has nothing to do except perform scale. Performance of scale is how small sites get cluttered.

Google's guidance on people-first content asks whether a page has a real audience and whether a reader leaves having learned something. It also warns against adding content to seem fresh or substantial. An empty newsroom fails both tests. It is there so the footer looks like a larger company's footer. That is not a reader.

One mention does not require a system. Put it on the about page. "Featured in" followed by the name and a link is honest and small. When you have a pattern, several mentions or a real sequence of company news, give them a page. Until then, the pattern is a wish.

Do not backfill the wish with posts. "We redesigned our homepage" is not news unless your buyers are your peers and you have something to teach. A diary of internal milestones, published to keep a press page from looking empty, makes the company look inward. Ship the work. Write when the writing helps someone who is not you.

## What a small page can hold

When you do have the materials, keep the page short. A paragraph that says what the company does, in the same words as the homepage. A contact that a person reads, not a black hole. Links to the original stories, with the publication, the title, and the date. If you have a fact sheet, make it a fact sheet: what you offer, where you are based if that matters, and how to reach you.

Offer logo files only if people ask, and offer the current ones. A zip of three versions, with a sentence about clear space, is plenty. Do not build a brand portal for imaginary press. The client portal you use with actual clients is a different tool, for their files. The public press page is a shelf, not a product.

Boilerplate can be one sentence and one longer paragraph. Write it the way you would want it copied. If you would cringe to see the long version in print, it is too ornate. Plain description copies well. Adjectives get cut by editors anyway, often in a way that makes you look more inflated than if you had been plain.

Dates matter. A page whose newest item is two years old tells the truth, and the truth may be that you have been heads-down. You can leave the items up if they are still accurate. You should not pin a "latest news" label on a stale post. If nothing has happened, say who you are and how to reach you, and let the archive be an archive. Rename the heading. "Selected mentions" is calmer than "Newsroom" when you are not a newsroom.

## The about page can carry the real mentions

The about page is where a buyer goes to see if people stand behind the offer. A few links belong there naturally, next to the description of the studio or the company. They support the "who," which is the question that page is for. A separate press section splits that proof into a room that then needs feeding.

Link to the original, and use the publication's name. Do not copy the article onto your site. You usually do not have the right, and a reprint looks like you are manufacturing a library. A title, a date, and a link are the respectful version. If the piece is gone, do not pretend the link works. Remove it or point at a saved description in your own words, clearly marked as yours.

If a founder was quoted, attribute the quote to the piece, with the date. Do not pull the quote into a testimonial slot as if the journalist were a client. Different relationships, different shelves. Mixing them is how a press mention gets inflated into an endorsement the writer did not make.

Keep the tone even. "As seen in" with one local newsletter and a global masthead side by side, in identical lockups, looks like a trick. You can list both. Let the names speak at a readable size, and skip the fireworks. The reader knows the difference. Your job is not to disguise it.

## What journalists actually need

They need a fast answer. What the company is. Why this note is relevant. Who to email. A way to check the spelling of the name and the product. They do not need a mission video. If you are sending a pitch, the pitch is the email. The page is the check they do if the email was interesting.

Put a named contact if you can. A founder is a legitimate press contact at a small company. Say so. "Email the founder" is more credible than a form that says "media inquiries" and routes to the same inbox as support, unlabeled. If you use a form, the confirmation should say who reads it and when, the same as any other form.

Have the facts straight before you invite the contact. A page that says you are in ten countries when you have ten users in one city will be discovered. Correct the marketing site first. Press does not fix a fuzzy offer. It amplifies it. A clear, small description is safer than a large, soft one.

Respond when they write, even with a no. Silence from an address you published as press is a bigger story than a short reply. You do not owe an interview. You owe the path you printed. If the address is not watched, take it off the page.

## Do not manufacture a beat

A steady cadence of nothing is still nothing. Product tweaks, hiring posts with no role attached, and "we're excited to announce" with no news under it train readers to ignore you. They also clutter the site with thin URLs. Prefer a quiet year and one page that is true to a monthly drip you would not read yourself.

Awards you did not win, lists you paid to join, and badges from directories are not press. They can sit in a footer if you insist and the terms allow. They should not lead a news page. A buyer who knows the badge knows the transaction. Lead with the work.

Founder essays belong in a journal if they are useful to your readers. They do not become press because you put them in a "News" category. Call the journal a journal. Call a mention a mention. The labels are part of the honesty. Google's own distinction between people-first writing and writing that exists to look abundant is a good internal test. Who is this for, if they arrive with a question? If the answer is "for the impression of motion," do not publish it.

When something real happens, a launch, a paper, a change a customer must know, write it up in plain sentences and date it. That post can live on the journal and be linked from about. You still may not need a newsroom. The URL of a true post is enough to send.

## When the page becomes worth it

You will know, because people will ask. A partner wants the boilerplate. A writer wants the logo. You have more than one mention and they are getting hard to find. That is the moment to make a simple page, not a moment sooner. The design can match the about page. It does not need its own visual language, a masonry grid, or a subscribe modal.

Keep maintaining it or take it down. A press page is a promise of currency in a way an about page is not. If you will not update it, do not launch it. Put the links where you already update the description of the company. Maintenance is the cost of the nav item.

Look at your navigation with a stranger's eyes. If "Press" sits beside "Work" and "Contact" and contains less information than either, it is stealing a slot. Navigation is a short list of what you actually offer. News is rarely one of the three things a small company needs a buyer to find first.
